title: THE MOST DANGEROUS WAY TO LOSE JESUS IS TO THINK YOU’RE FOLLOWING HIM
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS WAY TO LOSE JESUS IS TO THINK YOU’RE FOLLOWING HIM
Are We Following Jesus—or Just Following Christians Who Talk About Jesus? The Uncomfortable Truth About Borrowed Faith, Spiritual Blindness, and the Savior We May Have Never Truly Known.
There is something terrifying about the possibility of spending years around Christianity… and never truly surrendering your life to Christ.
You can know the worship songs.
You can recognize the famous preachers.
You can quote the verses everyone shares.
You can defend your church, admire your pastor, follow Christian influencers, and fill your Facebook feed with messages about God.
You can even become the person everyone calls when they need spiritual advice.
And still, somewhere beneath all that religious activity, there may be a question you have been avoiding.
If every Christian voice you admired suddenly disappeared tomorrow, would you still know how to follow Jesus?
Not your pastor's Jesus.
Not your favorite preacher's Jesus.
Not the Jesus presented in a thirty-second motivational video.
Not the Jesus who conveniently agrees with everything you already believe.
The Jesus of Scripture.
The Jesus who loved sinners without approving their sin.
The Jesus who confronted religious hypocrisy without abandoning holiness.
The Jesus who welcomed the broken, called the proud to repentance, washed the feet of His disciples, and willingly went to the cross for people who could never save themselves.
Would you recognize Him?
Or have you become so familiar with people talking about Jesus that you have mistaken their voices for His?
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.
Because one of the most dangerous things that can happen to a Christian is not necessarily walking away from religion.
Sometimes it is remaining deeply involved in religion while slowly losing sight of the One religion is supposed to lead us toward.
And the frightening part?
You may not even notice it happening.
Jesus once confronted people who were extraordinarily serious about Scripture.
They studied it. They respected it. They believed it testified to eternal life.
Yet He said something devastating.
In John 5:39–40, Jesus told them that the Scriptures bore witness about Him, but they refused to come to Him to have life.
Think about that.
They possessed the sacred writings that pointed toward the Messiah, yet they resisted the Messiah standing before them.
Their problem was not that they knew too much Scripture.
Their problem was that they would not respond rightly to the One Scripture revealed.
And before we shake our heads at them, perhaps we should ask ourselves a painful question.
Could we be doing something similar?
Could we be collecting sermons without practicing obedience?
Defending Christian personalities without examining their teaching?
Quoting verses about forgiveness while refusing to forgive?
Posting about holiness while protecting secret compromises?
Talking about the love of Christ while treating wounded people with contempt?
Could we be defending Christianity publicly while resisting Christ privately?
I remember the kind of question that can make an entire room go quiet.
Imagine someone who has attended church for twenty years.
They have served on committees, donated faithfully, memorized Bible passages, and listened to hundreds of sermons.
Then someone asks them, quietly:
"When was the last time you obeyed Jesus when nobody was watching?"
Silence.
Not because church attendance, service, giving, and biblical knowledge are worthless.
They are not.
But because none of those things can replace a heart that actually belongs to Christ.
A person can learn the language of discipleship without living as a disciple.
And that is precisely why Jesus' words in Matthew 7:21 are so sobering:
"Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven." (KJV)
He was not teaching that we purchase salvation through good behavior.
He was exposing the terrible difference between a profession of faith and a genuine relationship with Him.
A mouth can say "Lord" while a heart continues to insist, "I will rule my own life."
That is the scandal of counterfeit discipleship.
And it is not merely someone else's problem.
It is a warning for all of us.
The Greek language of the New Testament gives us a remarkable window into what following Jesus actually means.
When Jesus called His first disciples in Matthew 4:19, He said:
Δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου
Deute opisō mou.
"Come after me."
The expression is an invitation to follow behind Him.
Not to admire Him from a distance.
Not to make Him a decorative addition to an otherwise unchanged life.
Not to follow another person merely because that person speaks confidently about Him.
To come after Jesus Himself.
And in Luke 9:23, Jesus deepens the invitation with words that should dismantle every comfortable imitation of discipleship:
"Let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (KJV)
The Greek verb translated "follow" is ἀκολουθείτω (akoloutheitō), a present imperative in this passage, expressing the command to follow Him as an ongoing way of life.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
"Follow whoever has the largest audience."
"Follow whoever makes you feel spiritually superior."
"Follow whoever promises you a life without suffering."
"Follow whoever speaks most passionately, even if their teaching contradicts My Word."
No.
He said, "Follow me."
And that changes everything.
Because following Jesus means His truth has authority over our preferences.
His commands matter more than our excuses.
His character becomes the standard by which we evaluate those who claim to represent Him.
Even the Christian leaders we admire most.
Especially them.
The apostle Paul understood this.
In 1 Corinthians 11:1, he wrote:
"Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ." (KJV)
The Greek expression μιμηταί μου γίνεσθε (mimētai mou ginesthe) means, in context, "be imitators of me."
But Paul immediately places a crucial qualification on that invitation.
As I also am of Christ.
Paul was not asking believers to give him unquestioning allegiance.
He was pointing them toward a pattern of life shaped by Jesus.
His example mattered because it was meant to reflect Christ.
And that gives us an important principle.
A faithful Christian leader is not someone who makes you increasingly dependent on their personality.
A faithful Christian leader helps you become increasingly grounded in Jesus Christ.
A good pastor does not need to be your savior.
A faithful teacher does not need to be treated as infallible.
A Christian influencer does not need to become the final authority over your conscience.
And a church community, however precious, must never take the place that belongs to Christ alone.
We need pastors.
We need teachers.
We need spiritual mentors.
We need the church.
Scripture itself teaches that Christ gives leaders to equip His people for ministry and maturity (Ephesians 4:11–16).
This is not an invitation to abandon Christian community, distrust every minister, or imagine that spiritual independence is the same as spiritual maturity.
But every genuine ministry must remain accountable to the Lord it claims to serve.
Because the moment a human voice becomes more authoritative to us than the Word of God, something has gone terribly wrong.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
You trusted someone.
Maybe it was a pastor whose sermons helped you through your darkest season.
Maybe it was a Christian friend who prayed with you when your marriage was falling apart.
Maybe it was a ministry leader who taught you how to read the Bible.
Maybe it was a believer whose public life seemed so holy that you assumed their private life must be equally beautiful.
You admired them.
You defended them.
You believed them.
Then something happened.
A lie came to light.
An abuse of trust was exposed.
A leader manipulated someone vulnerable.
A Christian who preached forgiveness treated you with cruelty.
A person who constantly spoke about righteousness was discovered living in deliberate hypocrisy.
And suddenly, the faith you thought was solid began to tremble.
Not merely because someone disappointed you.
But because somewhere along the way, you had allowed that person to become part of the foundation of your faith.
And when they fell, it felt as though Jesus had fallen with them.
If you have experienced that kind of spiritual betrayal, please hear this carefully.
What happened to you matters.
The wounds caused by hypocrisy, manipulation, and spiritual abuse should never be dismissed with a careless command to "just forgive and move on."
Forgiveness does not require pretending evil was harmless.
Grace does not cancel accountability.
And honoring God never requires protecting a leader from legitimate scrutiny or consequences.
But there is something else you need to know.
The failure of someone who represents Jesus does not mean Jesus Himself has failed.
The betrayal of Judas did not make Christ a betrayer.
Peter's denial did not make Christ unfaithful.
The disciples' fear did not make Christ cowardly.
And the failures of Christians today do not change the character of the Savior revealed in Scripture.
Jesus has never needed His followers to be perfect in order for Him to remain holy.
That does not excuse our failures.
It makes repentance all the more necessary.
Because the same Jesus who restores sinners also confronts those who use religion to exploit, deceive, or crush others.
Look at Matthew 23.
Jesus spoke some of His strongest words against religious leaders whose outward appearance concealed inward corruption.
In Matthew 23:27, He compared them to whitewashed tombs.
Beautiful on the outside.
Full of death within.
It is a frightening picture.
And it should make every one of us examine the distance between the person we present publicly and the person we are privately.
Because hypocrisy does not begin only when someone becomes famous.
Sometimes it begins quietly.
With a Christian post we share but refuse to practice.
With an apology we know we owe but will not offer.
With a secret sin we excuse because nobody knows.
With a cruel attitude we defend because we believe we are doctrinally correct.
With a religious image we protect more fiercely than our actual relationship with God.
And perhaps the most dangerous part of hypocrisy is that, after enough time, we can begin believing our own performance.
We mistake being perceived as spiritual for being spiritually healthy.
We mistake knowing the correct answers for having a surrendered heart.
We mistake being surrounded by Christian activity for abiding in Christ.
But Jesus is not impressed by a carefully maintained religious reputation.
He sees the heart.
He sees the person who cries alone after smiling through an entire church service.
He sees the believer who has grown cold but is terrified to admit it.
He sees the Christian who has learned to argue theology but forgotten how to love.
He sees the exhausted servant who is doing everything for the ministry while barely spending time with the Master.
And He sees the wounded soul who wants to believe again but no longer knows whom to trust.
To that soul, the invitation of Jesus remains astonishingly tender.
In Matthew 11:28, He says:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (KJV)
Not "Come to the most impressive religious personality."
Not "Come when you have repaired your reputation."
Not "Come when you have finally become good enough."
Come unto me.
The Greek words are Δεῦτε πρός με (Deute pros me).
"Come to me."
The invitation is personal.
And that matters more than we sometimes realize.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about finding flawless Christians.
It is about being reconciled to the holy God through Jesus Christ, the crucified and risen Savior.
It is about grace that does not deny sin but provides forgiveness through the cross.
It is about a Savior who does not merely teach us how to appear righteous but gives new life to those who trust Him.
And it is about the Holy Spirit transforming us into people whose lives increasingly reflect Christ.
But here is another uncomfortable truth.
Some of us are not following Christian leaders because they help us obey Jesus.
We follow them because they help us avoid the parts of Jesus' teaching we do not want to obey.
We prefer the preacher who never confronts our greed.
The teacher who never challenges our bitterness.
The influencer who always confirms our political, cultural, or personal assumptions.
The voice that tells us we are always the victim, never the one who needs repentance.
The message that promises blessings without surrender, victory without endurance, and spiritual growth without correction.
And when someone opens Scripture and challenges us, we dismiss them.
Not because they are necessarily wrong.
But because the truth threatens the version of Christianity we have constructed around ourselves.
Paul warned Timothy that people would gather teachers according to their own desires rather than endure sound teaching (2 Timothy 4:3–4).
That warning deserves serious attention in an age when we can choose exactly which voices appear on our screens.
With a single tap, we can silence anyone who challenges us.
With another, we can find someone who makes our favorite excuses sound biblical.
We can build an entire digital world where every religious voice tells us what we want to hear.
And still call it discipleship.
But spiritual maturity does not mean finding teachers who always agree with us.
It means learning to recognize truth, receive correction, and submit to Christ even when His Word exposes something we would rather hide.
Consider the believers in Berea.
Acts 17:11 describes how they received Paul's message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to see whether what he taught was true.
Think about that.
They were listening to the apostle Paul.
Yet their careful examination of Scripture was commended.
They were neither cynical nor gullible.
They were receptive and discerning.
That is a beautiful model for us.
Listen to faithful teachers.
Learn from mature believers.
Receive biblical correction.
Participate in a healthy local church.
But open your Bible.
Read passages in context.
Ask whether the message truly reflects the meaning of Scripture.
Pay attention to the fruit of a leader's life.
And never confuse charisma with Christlikeness.
A powerful speaking voice is not proof of spiritual maturity.
A large following is not proof of divine approval.
An emotional sermon is not automatically faithful teaching.
A verified account is not a certificate of holiness.
And an impressive ministry does not place anyone beyond accountability.
Jesus taught that people could be recognized by their fruits (Matthew 7:15–20).
That requires more than judging a person by a single moment, rumor, or online accusation.
It calls for careful, truthful discernment of teaching, conduct, character, and patterns over time.
Because not everyone who speaks beautifully about Jesus lives faithfully before Him.
And not everyone who quietly follows Jesus will ever become famous.
Sometimes the most Christlike person in a congregation is the elderly widow who prays when nobody notices.
The father who asks his children for forgiveness after losing his temper.
The woman who refuses to return cruelty for cruelty.
The young believer who deletes a dishonest message and chooses truth even though lying would have been easier.
The worker who refuses to steal when nobody is watching.
The wounded Christian who takes one trembling step toward trusting Christ again.
No spotlight.
No viral testimony.
No impressive platform.
Just grace doing its patient work in an ordinary human heart.
And heaven does not measure faithfulness by the number of people who applaud.
There is a moment in John's Gospel that feels almost painfully relevant to our generation.
In John 21, after the resurrection, Jesus spoke with Peter.
Peter had denied Him three times.
He had failed publicly and painfully.
Yet the risen Christ was not finished with him.
Jesus restored Peter and called him to follow.
Then Peter noticed another disciple and asked Jesus about that man's future.
Jesus answered in John 21:22:
"What is that to thee? follow thou me." (KJV)
Read that again.
"What is that to thee? follow thou me."
Jesus was not forbidding Peter from caring about others.
He was correcting Peter's distraction from his own calling.
Peter wanted to know about someone else's path.
Jesus redirected him to his own responsibility.
How many of us need to hear that today?
We know what our favorite preacher posted this morning.
But we have not opened the Gospel of John in weeks.
We know which Christian influencer is arguing with another influencer.
But we have ignored the person in our own home who needs our kindness.
We know the latest controversy involving a ministry.
But we have not confessed the resentment quietly growing in our hearts.
We can spend hours debating whether another Christian is faithful while refusing to ask whether we ourselves are obeying Christ.
And Jesus still says:
Not because truth and accountability do not matter.
They do.
But because another person's discipleship cannot substitute for your own.
Your pastor cannot repent on your behalf.
Your favorite Christian author cannot trust Christ for you.
Your parents' faith cannot become your faith merely through inheritance.
Your church membership cannot replace the new birth.
Your online religious identity cannot make your heart right with God.
And your ability to recognize someone else's hypocrisy does not automatically make you holy.
Every one of us must come to Jesus.
Every one of us needs His mercy.
Every one of us must hear His call.
And that brings us to the deepest question of this entire conversation.
What if the real problem is not simply that we have been following the wrong Christians?
What if we have been using other Christians to avoid facing Jesus Himself?
Because Jesus is not merely an inspiring figure whose teachings can be selected according to personal taste.
He is Lord.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He commands us to love our enemies.
He teaches us to forgive.
He exposes pride.
He confronts greed.
He calls us to purity, humility, truthfulness, and costly love.
And He refuses to become the mascot of our self-centered ambitions.
Following Jesus is beautiful.
But it is not always comfortable.
Sometimes it means admitting that the person you criticized was right.
Sometimes it means returning money you dishonestly took.
Sometimes it means ending a secret relationship you know dishonors God.
Sometimes it means apologizing to the child you wounded.
Sometimes it means refusing to join a cruel conversation, even when everyone else is laughing.
Sometimes it means speaking truth when silence would preserve your popularity.
And sometimes it means leaving an unhealthy religious environment while continuing to cling to Christ.
None of these acts earns the salvation Jesus purchased.
But genuine faith is not indifferent to the One it calls Lord.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds together two truths we must never separate.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
And we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not the reward for successful discipleship.
Grace is the undeserved gift that saves us and begins transforming our lives.
That is why the Gospel is so much more than a demand to become a better person.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience where we have failed.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
And He rose again, just as the Scriptures declare (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He did not come merely to improve our religious image.
He came to reconcile us to God.
And no Christian celebrity, pastor, ministry, church tradition, or personal achievement can take His place.
Only Jesus is the mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).
Only Jesus is the Savior.
Only Jesus is worthy of our ultimate allegiance.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because Peter failed.
And Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted.
And the risen Christ met him with evidence and an invitation to believe.
Paul persecuted the church.
And the Lord showed him extraordinary mercy, transforming a persecutor into a servant of the Gospel.
Their stories do not teach that sin is insignificant.
They reveal that Christ's mercy is greater than the sinner's past and that His grace produces a changed direction.
Perhaps you are reading this with a secret shame.
You used to pray.
You used to love Scripture.
You used to feel joy when someone mentioned Jesus.
But somewhere along the way, disappointment became distance.
Distance became indifference.
And indifference became a life in which Jesus is still part of your vocabulary but no longer at the center of your decisions.
You still share Christian content.
You still say "God bless you."
You still believe that Jesus is real.
But privately, you know something has changed.
You have been surviving on memories of a relationship with God instead of actively walking with Him.
And you are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of comparing yourself with other believers.
Tired of religious arguments.
Tired of performing strength while carrying spiritual emptiness.
If that is you, do not turn this moment into another opportunity to condemn yourself and then continue unchanged.
Turn to Christ.
Confess what is true.
Ask for mercy.
Open His Word again.
Seek the support of trustworthy believers.
Take the next step of obedience that His Word has made clear.
Not because God is waiting for you to manufacture a perfect spiritual performance.
But because Jesus is a sufficient Savior for repentant sinners.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
There is no need to keep hiding behind a religious image when you can come honestly before the Lord.
And if your faith has been shaken by the sins of others, you do not have to pretend that your wounds have disappeared.
Healing may require time.
It may require wise counsel.
It may require boundaries and accountability.
It may require stepping away from people who have abused their spiritual influence.
But even in that painful process, you can begin learning the difference between the voice of a harmful person and the voice of the Good Shepherd.
In John 10:27, Jesus says:
"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me." (KJV)
The Greek text reads:
τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.
Ta probata ta ema tēs phōnēs mou akouousin, kagō ginōskō auta, kai akolouthousin moi.
"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
In its context, this is not a promise that every private impression or inner thought is a direct message from God.
Jesus is describing the relationship between Himself and those who belong to Him.
They recognize and respond to their Shepherd.
They are known by Him.
And they follow Him.
Notice the tenderness of those words.
"I know them."
The Savior does not merely count His sheep.
He knows them.
He knows the believer whose prayers have become whispers.
He knows the young Christian confused by competing religious voices.
He knows the parent trying to lead a family while struggling privately.
He knows the person who has been hurt by church leaders.
He knows the one who has fallen into sin and desperately needs to repent.
He knows the believer who is afraid that faith will never feel the same again.
And He calls His people to follow Him.
Not an algorithm.
Not a personality.
Not a spiritual performance.
Him.
Perhaps the greatest evidence that someone is helping you follow Jesus is not that you become more impressed with that person.
It is that you become more devoted to Christ.
You begin reading Scripture with greater care.
You become more willing to repent.
You grow in love for other people.
You become less interested in appearing superior.
You learn to discern truth without becoming cruel.
You discover that obedience matters even when nobody is applauding.
And you become increasingly grateful that your salvation rests on the grace of Jesus rather than your ability to maintain a flawless reputation.
That is the kind of discipleship worth pursuing.
And it is the kind of discipleship Gospel Warrior longs to encourage.
Not a community built around worshiping a ministry.
Not a platform where human personalities become untouchable.
Not a place where popularity is mistaken for spiritual authority.
But a growing community of people who want to know Scripture, follow Jesus, confront sin honestly, receive grace humbly, and help others discover the hope of the Gospel.
That is why we continue creating and sharing biblical reflections, Christian teaching, devotional material, and resources intended to strengthen believers in their daily walk with Christ.
These resources are offered because spiritual nourishment should not be reduced to a privilege reserved for people who can afford it.
And if this article has helped you see something in your walk with God that you had not recognized before, please do not let that realization disappear beneath the next notification.
Not as another religious post you will never revisit, but as something to return to when the noise of competing voices becomes overwhelming.
A single thoughtful share can place biblical encouragement in front of someone who might never search for it on their own.
If Jesus examined your life today, would He find someone following Him—or someone mainly following people who talk about Him?
You do not have to answer that question publicly.
But please answer it honestly before God.
You do not need to reveal private details, painful experiences, or anything that could compromise your safety.
Sometimes a few honest words can open the door to meaningful prayer and fellowship.
And if God has carried you through a season of spiritual disappointment, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Someone reading may be wondering whether faith can survive betrayal.
Your testimony may remind them that Jesus remains faithful even when people are not.
There is also another way you can help this mission continue.

It is a voluntary opportunity to help sustain and expand a ministry devoted to sharing the Gospel, encouraging believers, developing discipleship resources, and reaching people who may be spiritually isolated or searching for hope.
Scripture encourages cheerful, willing giving rather than giving under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And it recognizes the importance of supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6; Philippians 4:15–18).
But there is an important distinction we must honor.
Your commitment to your local church, your family responsibilities, and your own circumstances deserve thoughtful consideration.
And the grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
You can still pray, learn, share the free resources, encourage others, and help the message reach more people.
These products are not substitutes for Scripture or spiritual growth. They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and support the ongoing work.
Because sometimes the person who needs to hear about Jesus is not searching for a sermon.
They are simply scrolling through their feed, carrying a pain nobody knows about.
They may be one message away from reconsidering the Christ they thought they had lost when a Christian disappointed them.
They may be one Scripture passage away from recognizing a truth they have avoided.
They may be one invitation away from opening a Bible again.
We cannot guarantee what any single article or share will accomplish.
But we can faithfully place the truth before people and trust God with the results.
And now, before this article ends, I want to bring you back to where we began.
Imagine that tomorrow every Christian voice you admire becomes silent.
No sermons from your favorite preacher.
No livestreams.
No Christian influencers.
No devotional notifications.
No inspiring quotes.
No one to tell you what to think.
Only you.
Your Bible.
And the question Jesus placed before His disciples.
In Matthew 16:15, He asked:
"But whom say ye that I am?" (KJV)
That question has never stopped mattering.
Not "Who does your pastor say I am?"
Not "Who does your favorite Christian personality say I am?"
Not "What does the crowd say about Me?"
Who do you say that I am?
Peter answered that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of the living God.
And that confession points us to the heart of everything.
Christianity does not stand or fall on the perfection of Christians.
It stands on the identity, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Christian leaders may disappoint us.
Churches may need correction.
Believers may stumble.
Some people who claim Christ may reveal through their actions that they have never truly submitted to Him.
And we ourselves may discover areas of deep compromise that require repentance.
But Jesus Christ remains the same.
He is not less holy because someone used His name dishonestly.
He is not less merciful because someone who claimed to represent Him acted without compassion.
He is not less truthful because someone twisted Scripture.
And He is not less worthy of following because human beings have failed.
The answer to counterfeit Christianity is not to abandon the real Christ.
It is to return to Him.
To His Word.
To His cross.
To His resurrection.
To His grace.
To His call to repent, believe, and follow.
Maybe you have spent years watching Christians.
Maybe you have spent years defending Christians.
Maybe you have spent years being disappointed by Christians.
Maybe you have even spent years pretending to be the kind of Christian everyone expects you to be.
But today, the question is no longer what everyone else is doing.
The question is what you will do with Jesus.
Will you keep hiding behind someone else's faith?
Will you keep excusing your disobedience because another believer failed?
Will you keep allowing the sins of human beings to determine your understanding of the sinless Savior?
Or will you finally come to Him as you are, confessing your need for mercy and trusting the One who gave His life to redeem sinners?
Because the greatest Christian testimony is not, "Look how impressive my spiritual leader is."
It is not, "Look how perfect my church appears."
It is not even, "Look how much I have accomplished for God."
It is this:
"I was a sinner in need of grace, and Jesus Christ is my Savior."
That is where pride begins to die.
That is where repentance becomes honest.
That is where grace becomes precious.
That is where a borrowed religious identity gives way to personal faith in Christ.
And that is where the story can begin to change.
Not because you finally found Christians who will never disappoint you.
But because you have come to the Savior who never sins, never lies, never betrays His promises, and never ceases to be worthy of your trust.
So follow faithful Christians as they follow Christ.
Love the church without idolizing it.
Honor pastors without treating them as infallible.
Receive teaching without abandoning discernment.
Practice accountability without becoming consumed by suspicion.
And when someone you admire falls, do not use their failure as permission to walk away from the One who died for you.
Look to Jesus.
When you are confused, look to Jesus.
When you are ashamed, come to Jesus.
When you are tempted to perform righteousness instead of pursuing holiness, return to Jesus.
When the world becomes loud and every voice claims to speak for God, open the Scriptures and seek to know Jesus more faithfully.
Because in the end, the question is not whether you knew the most famous Christians.
It is whether you truly belonged to Christ.
And perhaps the words your soul most needs to hear today are the same words the risen Savior spoke to Peter.
"Follow thou me."
Not the crowd.
Not the celebrity.
Not the performance.
Not the religious image you have spent years protecting.
Jesus.
Only Jesus is worthy of the throne of your heart.
And if you have wandered, His Gospel still calls you to repent and believe.
If you have fallen, His grace is sufficient to receive the sinner who turns to Him.
If you have been wounded, His truth remains trustworthy even when those who claimed to represent Him were not.
If you have become distracted, His Word can redirect your steps.
And if your life has become a story of shame, regret, spiritual confusion, or painful failure, remember what the cross and empty tomb declare.
Your sin is serious.
His mercy is real.
And through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life are possible.
You can spend your whole life standing in the shadows of people who speak about the Light—and never turn your face toward the One who came to save you.
